flashcards.front: When does the excess property check fire?
flashcards.back: Only for a fresh object literal assigned straight to a typed target; it exists to catch misspelled properties.

flashcards.front: Why prefer unknown over any for external data?
flashcards.back: unknown forces a check before use, while any silently disables type checking wherever the value flows.

flashcards.front: Five ways to narrow a union
flashcards.back: typeof, instanceof, an in check, comparing a discriminant tag, and a user-defined type guard function.

flashcards.front: What is a discriminated union?
flashcards.back: A union whose variants share a literal tag property, so checking the tag narrows to exactly one variant.

flashcards.front: How do you get exhaustiveness checking?
flashcards.back: In the fallback branch, assign the narrowed value to a variable of type never; any unhandled variant becomes a compile error.

flashcards.front: Do TypeScript types validate request bodies?
flashcards.back: No. They are erased before running; validate at runtime with guards or a schema library and derive the type from the schema.

flashcards.front: What does as const do?
flashcards.back: It freezes inference: literal types instead of string or number, and readonly arrays, tuples and properties.

topics.title: TypeScript: generics & utility types
topics.summary: Generic functions and constraints, keyof and indexed access types, the utility types you use daily (Partial, Pick, Omit, Record, Readonly, ReturnType, Awaited), and deriving types instead of repeating them.
topics.lesson:
## Generics: types as parameters

```ts
function first<T>(xs: T[]): T | undefined { return xs[0]; }
first([1, 2])        // T inferred as number: returns number | undefined
first(['a'])         // string | undefined
```

A generic keeps the relationship between input and output. Without it you would write `any[] => any` and lose every check downstream. Inference does the work in most calls: `first([1, 2])` needs no `<number>`. Write the type argument only when there is nothing to infer from, as in `new Map<string, User>()` or `useState<User | null>(null)`.

**Constraints** say what a type parameter must have:

```ts
function byId<T extends { id: string }>(xs: T[], id: string): T | undefined {
  return xs.find((x) => x.id === id);   // x.id is allowed because of the constraint
}
byId([{ id: 1 }], '1');   // error: number is not assignable to string
```

## keyof and indexed access

```ts
type Keys = keyof { a: 1; b: 2 };           // 'a' | 'b'
function get<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K] { return obj[key]; }
get({ id: 1, name: 'x' }, 'name')            // string
get({ id: 1, name: 'x' }, 'nope')            // error
```

`T[K]` (indexed access) is "the type of property K of T".

`K extends keyof T` limits `key` to names that exist on the object, so a typo like `'nmae'` is a compile error instead of an `undefined` at runtime. The return type follows the key: `get(row, 'id')` is a number and `get(row, 'name')` a string, from one function and no overloads.

## The utility types

```ts
interface User { id: string; name: string; email: string; passwordHash: string }

Partial<User>                  // every property optional: PATCH bodies
Required<T>                    // every property required
Pick<User, 'id' | 'name'>      // only those keys
Omit<User, 'passwordHash'>     // everything except: public DTOs
Record<'draft' | 'live', number>  // an object with exactly those keys
Readonly<User>                 // assignments to properties are errors
ReturnType<typeof makeUser>    // the return type of a function
Awaited<Promise<Promise<string>>> // string: unwraps promises, recursively
NonNullable<string | null | undefined> // string
```

These are all compile-time only. `Readonly` does not freeze anything at runtime, and `Omit<User, 'passwordHash'>` does not remove the field from an object you send: you still have to build the DTO without it (`const { passwordHash, ...publicUser } = user`). A concrete trap: a handler declared as `(): Omit<User, 'passwordHash'>` that does `return user` compiles, because a value with more properties is assignable to the smaller type.

## Derive types instead of repeating them

Keep one source of truth and derive the rest:

```ts
const ROLES = ['admin', 'editor', 'viewer'] as const;
type Role = (typeof ROLES)[number];            // 'admin' | 'editor' | 'viewer'

type CreateUser = Omit<User, 'id'>;            // POST body
type UpdateUser = Partial<CreateUser>;         // PATCH body
type UserRow = Awaited<ReturnType<typeof db.users.findFirst>>;
```

Change `User` once and every derived type follows. Add `'auditor'` to `ROLES` and `Role` gains it, so every `switch` over a role with a `never` check stops compiling until it handles the new value. A hand-written union kept next to the array drifts away from it silently.

## Mapped and conditional types (reading level)

`Partial` is itself a mapped type: `{ [K in keyof T]?: T[K] }`. Conditional types branch on types: `T extends string ? 'text' : 'other'`. You will read them in library typings more than you write them. A conditional type applied to a union checks each member separately: `T extends null ? never : T` turns `string | null` into `string`.

## Where generics show up in CRUD code

A typed API client `get<T>(url): Promise<T>` (remember: the `T` is an unchecked claim about the response, not a validation), repository interfaces `Repo<T extends { id: string }>`, React components `<Select<T> items={T[]} />`, and `Result<T, E>` unions for error handling. In each case one type parameter ties several signatures together, so a change to `T` is checked everywhere it flows.

quiz.prompt: For `function pair<T>(x: T): [T, T]`, what is the type of `pair(5)`?
choices: `[number, number]`
`number[]`
`[unknown, unknown]`
quiz.explanation: T is inferred from the argument and the literal 5 widens to number, so the result is the tuple `[number, number]`; the signature keeps both the tuple shape and the link to T. `[5, 5]` would need a `const T` type parameter or an `as const` argument.

quiz.prompt: Why does `byId([{ id: 1 }], "1")` fail for `byId<T extends { id: string }>`?
choices: T cannot be inferred from an array of object literals
Generic functions cannot take array parameters
The element's id is a number, violating the constraint
The second argument "1" must be a number like the id
quiz.explanation: The constraint says every T must have a string id, and `{ id: 1 }` has a number id, so the argument does not satisfy `T extends { id: string }`. Inference from object literals works fine, and the "1" argument is not what fails: the element type is.

quiz.prompt: What is `keyof { a: 1; b: 2 }`?
choices: `string`
quiz.explanation: keyof gives the union of an object type's property NAMES, so it is `'a' | 'b'`. The values 1 | 2 would be `T[keyof T]`, and keyof never produces a tuple; `string` is what keyof gives for a type with a string index signature.

quiz.prompt: Which utility type best describes a PATCH body where any field may be sent?
choices: `Required<User>`
`Pick<User, "id">`
`Readonly<User>`
`Partial<User>`
quiz.explanation: A PATCH body may contain any subset of fields, and `Partial<User>` makes every property optional. Required makes them all mandatory, Pick<User, "id"> keeps only the id, and Readonly forbids assignment without making anything optional.

quiz.prompt: A `Record<"a" | "b", number>` is assigned `{ a: 1 }`. Result?
choices: Compiles: Record keys are optional
Error: property 'b' is missing
Compiles, and b defaults to 0
A runtime error when b is read
quiz.explanation: `Record<K, V>` is the mapped type `{ [P in K]: V }`, so every member of the key union becomes a required property. The literal has no `b`, and tsc rejects the assignment. Keys are not optional unless you wrap the Record in `Partial`, and TypeScript never fills in a default such as 0: types emit no code, so the check happens at compile time, not when b is read.

quiz.prompt: `res.json(user as Omit<User, "passwordHash">)` — is the hash removed from the response?
choices: Yes: Omit removes the field when the object is serialised
Yes in strict mode, where Omit is enforced at runtime
No: types are erased; the object still contains the field
Yes, if passwordHash is declared as an optional field
quiz.explanation: `as Omit<User, "passwordHash">` only changes what the compiler believes about the value. The emitted JavaScript is `res.json(user)`, and `JSON.stringify` writes every own enumerable property, the hash included. No strict mode setting or optional modifier changes that, because no type survives compilation. Remove the field from the data: `const { passwordHash, ...publicUser } = user;`, then send `publicUser`, or map the row to a DTO.

quiz.prompt: What is `Awaited<Promise<number> | string>`?
choices: `Promise<number> | string`
`string | number`
`Promise<string | number>`
`number`
quiz.explanation: Awaited distributes over a union and unwraps each promise member, while non-promise members pass through: `await` on a string gives the string. So the result is `string | number`, not `number` alone and not still a promise type.

quiz.prompt: `const ROLES = ["admin", "viewer"] as const; type Role = (typeof ROLES)[number];` What is Role?
choices: `'admin' | 'viewer'`
`string`
`readonly ['admin', 'viewer']`
`readonly string[]`
quiz.explanation: `as const` gives `ROLES` the type `readonly ['admin', 'viewer']`, a tuple whose elements keep their literal types. Indexing an array or tuple type with `number` asks for the type of any element, which for this tuple is the union of its two literals. Without `as const` the array would be `string[]` and Role would widen to `string`; the readonly tuple is the type of ROLES itself, not of one element.

quiz.prompt: Does `Readonly<User>` stop a property from being changed at runtime?
choices: Yes: it compiles to Object.freeze
Yes: strict mode throws on writes
Yes, for nested objects as well
No: it is a compile-time check only
quiz.explanation: `Readonly<User>` marks every property `readonly`, and that modifier lives only in the type: tsc reports an assignment as an error and emits the same JavaScript as before. Nothing calls `Object.freeze`, so code that goes around the type, through `as any` or plain JavaScript, can still write. It is also shallow: nested objects stay writable even in the type. Freeze the object when you need a runtime guarantee.

quiz.prompt: In `function get<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K]`, what does `T[K]` mean?
choices: An array of T values indexed by K
The type of property K of T
A tuple of T and K
Either the type K or the type T
quiz.explanation: An indexed access type looks up a property's type the way `obj[key]` looks up a value. With `K extends keyof T`, the call `get({ id: 1, name: 'x' }, 'name')` infers K as `'name'` and returns `string`, while the key `'id'` returns `number`. No array, tuple or either-or union is involved; the point is that the return type follows the key you pass.

flashcards.front: Why use a generic instead of any?
flashcards.back: A generic keeps the link between input and output types, so callers get precise types back; any discards checking everywhere it flows.

flashcards.front: What does a constraint like T extends { id: string } do?
flashcards.back: It limits which types may be used for T and lets the function body use the members the constraint guarantees.

flashcards.front: Partial, Required and Readonly
flashcards.back: Make every property optional, make every property mandatory, and forbid assignment to properties, all at compile time.

flashcards.front: Pick versus Omit
flashcards.back: Pick keeps only the named keys; Omit keeps all keys except the named ones.

flashcards.front: What does Record<K, V> describe?
flashcards.back: An object type with exactly the keys in K, each holding a V; with a union of literal keys, every key is required.

flashcards.front: ReturnType and Awaited together
flashcards.back: ReturnType reads a function's return type; wrapping it in Awaited unwraps the promise an async function returns.

flashcards.front: Do utility types change runtime objects?
flashcards.back: Never. An Omit type does not remove a field from the data; you still have to build the object without it.

flashcards.front: How do you turn a constant list into a union type?
flashcards.back: Declare the array with as const and index its type with number to get the union of its literal elements.

topics.title: Node core: fs, path, process, events & streams
topics.summary: The Node building blocks behind every backend: promise-based fs, path.join versus resolve, process.env strings, synchronous EventEmitter events and the error event, Buffers and bytes, and streams with backpressure.
topics.lesson:
## fs: use the promise API

```js
import { readFile, writeFile } from 'node:fs/promises';
const text = await readFile(new URL('./config.json', import.meta.url), 'utf8');
```

The `*Sync` functions block the whole process (topic 12): fine in a CLI or at startup, wrong inside a request handler. Relative paths in fs calls resolve against `process.cwd()` (where the process was started), NOT the file's folder; build paths from `import.meta.dirname` (or `__dirname` in CommonJS).

## path

```js
path.join('a', '../b')        // 'b'         joins and normalises
path.join('/a/', '/b')        // '/a/b'
path.resolve('/x', 'y', '../z') // '/x/z'    builds an ABSOLUTE path, right to left
path.resolve('/x', '/y')      // '/y'        a later absolute segment restarts
path.extname('a.tar.gz')      // '.gz'
```

Never concatenate paths with `+ '/'`; and never join untrusted input into a path without checking the result stays inside your base folder (path traversal: `../../etc/passwd`).

The check is concrete: with `const full = path.resolve(base, input)`, reject the request unless `full.startsWith(base + path.sep)`; for `input = '../../etc/passwd'` the resolved path is `/etc/passwd` and the check fails. On Windows the same calls produce backslashes, so compare with `path` functions, and use `path.posix.join` when you need `/`, as URLs and zip entries do.

## process

- `process.env` values are **always strings** (or undefined). `process.env.PORT = 3000` stores `'3000'`, and `'false'` is truthy. Parse and validate configuration once at startup.
- `process.argv`: `[nodePath, scriptPath, ...args]`.
- `process.exitCode = 1` lets the process finish its work and exit non-zero; `process.exit()` kills it immediately, possibly losing buffered output.
- Signals: listen for `SIGTERM` to shut down gracefully (stop accepting, finish in-flight requests, close the DB pool).

## EventEmitter

```js
const e = new EventEmitter();
e.on('saved', (doc) => log(doc.id));
e.emit('saved', doc);   // listeners run SYNCHRONOUSLY, in registration order, before emit returns
```

- `emit` returns `true` if there were listeners.
- `once` removes the listener after its first call.
- Emitting `'error'` with **no** `'error'` listener throws the error, which usually crashes the process. Always attach error listeners to streams, sockets and emitters you create.
- Forgetting to remove listeners in long-lived objects leaks memory (Node warns after 10 listeners for one event).

## Buffer: bytes, not characters

`Buffer.byteLength('é')` is 2 while `'é'.length` is 1. HTTP `Content-Length`, file sizes and database column limits count **bytes** in UTF-8. Splitting a Buffer at an arbitrary byte can cut a multi-byte character in half; decode text with a streaming decoder or by lines. Sizes grow quickly: `Buffer.from('€').length` is 3 and most emoji take 4 bytes.

## Streams and backpressure

Streams process data piece by piece: read a 5 GB file with constant memory. Readable streams are async iterables:

```js
import { pipeline } from 'node:stream/promises';
await pipeline(createReadStream('in.csv'), transformRows, createWriteStream('out.csv'));
```

`pipeline` connects streams, forwards errors from any stage and destroys every stream on failure. **Backpressure**: when a writable stream's buffer is full, `write()` returns false and the producer should wait for `'drain'`; `pipeline` and `for await` handle this for you, a manual `on('data')` loop does not. Chunks are arbitrary slices: a line or a JSON record can span two chunks, so keep the incomplete tail between chunks.

quiz.prompt: On Linux or macOS, what is `path.join('/app', 'src', '..', 'lib')`?
choices: `'/app/src/../lib'`
`'/app/src/lib'`
`'/app/lib/'`
`'/app/lib'`
quiz.explanation: join concatenates the segments and then normalises the result, so the `..` cancels `src` and no trailing slash is added. Keeping the `..` in the string, as in `'/app/src/../lib'`, is what plain string concatenation would give.

quiz.prompt: On Linux or macOS, what does `path.resolve('/srv', 'data', '/tmp', 'x')` return?
choices: `'/tmp/x'`
`'/srv/data/tmp/x'`
`'/srv/data//tmp/x'`
`'/srv/tmp/x'`
quiz.explanation: resolve works from right to left and stops at the first absolute segment it meets, here `/tmp`; everything to its left is ignored. Treating `/tmp` as one more relative piece, as in `'/srv/data/tmp/x'`, is how join would behave, not resolve.

quiz.prompt: After `process.env.FEATURE = false`, what is `typeof process.env.FEATURE` and is it truthy?
choices: 'boolean', falsy
'string', truthy
'undefined', falsy
'boolean', truthy
quiz.explanation: `process.env` is not an ordinary object: assigning to one of its properties converts the value to a string, so `false` is stored as `'false'` and `typeof` reports a string, never a boolean. Any non-empty string is truthy, so `if (process.env.FEATURE)` takes the true branch. Parse flags explicitly, for example `process.env.FEATURE === 'true'`, once at startup.

quiz.prompt: When do EventEmitter listeners run?
choices: In the next microtask, after emit() returns
On the next tick, scheduled with process.nextTick
After the current task, in reverse registration order
Synchronously, inside emit(), in registration order
quiz.explanation: `emit()` is a plain function call: it looks up the listener array for that event name and calls each listener in turn, in the order they were added, before it returns. No microtask, nextTick or later task is involved, so a slow or throwing listener runs inside the caller of `emit`. If work must happen later, defer it yourself with `setImmediate` or `queueMicrotask` inside the listener.

quiz.prompt: What happens on `emitter.emit("error", err)` when no "error" listener is registered?
choices: Nothing: the event is silently dropped
It returns false, like emit with no listeners
The error is thrown, typically crashing the process
It is logged as an unhandled-error warning on stderr
quiz.explanation: Node treats `'error'` as a special event name. When `emit('error', err)` finds no listener for it, it throws `err` right there, in the code that called emit, and an uncaught throw ends the process. The event is not dropped or merely logged as a warning, and emit does not return false the way it does for any other event nobody listens to. Attach an `'error'` listener to every emitter and stream you own.

quiz.prompt: What are `Buffer.byteLength('é')` and `'é'.length`?
choices: 1 and 1
2 and 2
1 and 2
2 and 1
quiz.explanation: `'é'` (U+00E9) is one UTF-16 code unit, so the string's `length` counts it once. `Buffer.byteLength` counts the bytes of the UTF-8 encoding, and every code point above U+007F needs at least two bytes there: é is `0xC3 0xA9`. The two functions count different things. Using `length` for a Content-Length header or a byte-limited column is a classic mistake.

quiz.prompt: A relative path in `readFile("./data.json")` is resolved against...
choices: The current working directory of the process
The folder of the file that calls readFile
The project root, where package.json lives
The home directory of the current user
quiz.explanation: fs functions hand a relative path to the operating system, which resolves it against the process's current working directory, `process.cwd()`. That is wherever the process was started, so `node src/app.js` run from the project root and from `src/` reads different files. Node does not look at the calling file's folder or search for package.json. Build source-relative paths from `import.meta.dirname` or `__dirname`.

quiz.prompt: Why use `pipeline()` instead of chaining `.pipe()` calls?
choices: It is faster, since data skips the intermediate buffers
It propagates errors and destroys all streams on failure
pipe() was removed from the stream API in Node 18
It compresses data automatically between each pair of stages
quiz.explanation: `.pipe()` forwards data and backpressure but not errors: when the transform in the middle fails, the source and the destination are left open, and each stream needs its own `'error'` listener. `pipeline()` listens to every stage, destroys all of them on the first failure, and reports that one error to a single callback or promise. It does not compress anything and is not faster, and `.pipe()` still exists.

quiz.prompt: What is backpressure?
choices: Compressing chunks so the stream moves faster
Retrying writes that failed on the destination
The consumer signalling the producer to slow down
Reading a file from the end towards the start
quiz.explanation: write() returns false when the buffer is full; producers should wait for drain. pipeline and for await handle it. The consumer asks the producer to pause because its buffer is full.

quiz.prompt: Why can a readable stream of text split a line in two?
choices: Chunks are arbitrary slices, not aligned to lines
Line breaks are dropped when chunks are decoded
Backpressure pauses the stream in the middle of lines
It cannot: streams in text mode emit whole lines
quiz.explanation: A readable stream hands out whatever the source produced: a file stream reads 64 KiB blocks, and a socket delivers whatever arrived. Neither knows about newlines, so a chunk can end halfway through a line, or even inside a multi-byte character. Nothing drops line breaks, backpressure only delays chunks, and there is no text mode that emits whole lines. Keep the trailing partial line for the next chunk, or use `readline`.

flashcards.front: path.join versus path.resolve
flashcards.back: join glues segments and normalises them; resolve builds an absolute path, starting over at the right-most absolute segment.

flashcards.front: What type are environment variables?
flashcards.back: Always strings or undefined. Numbers and booleans must be parsed, and the string false is still truthy.

flashcards.front: process.exit() versus process.exitCode
flashcards.back: exit stops immediately and can drop buffered output; setting exitCode lets pending work finish and then exits with that code.

flashcards.front: How does EventEmitter deliver events?
flashcards.back: Synchronously during emit, to every listener in the order they were added.

flashcards.front: Why attach an error listener to every stream and emitter?
flashcards.back: An error event with no listener is thrown, which normally brings down the whole process.

flashcards.front: Bytes versus characters in Node
flashcards.back: Content-Length, file sizes and many column limits count UTF-8 bytes; JavaScript string length counts UTF-16 code units.

flashcards.front: What does stream.pipeline give you?
flashcards.back: Streams wired together with backpressure, errors from any stage propagated, and every stream cleaned up on failure.

flashcards.front: Why avoid the Sync fs functions in request handlers?
flashcards.back: They block the single JavaScript thread, so every other request waits until the file operation finishes.

topics.title: HTTP APIs in Node
topics.summary: Methods and idempotency, the status codes that matter, routes and query strings, middleware order and error middleware, validating bodies at the boundary, and pagination.
topics.lesson:
## Methods and their promises

| method | use | safe | idempotent |
|---|---|---|---|
| GET | read | yes | yes |
| POST | create / run an action | no | no |
| PUT | replace a resource at a known URL | no | yes |
| PATCH | partial update | no | not necessarily |
| DELETE | remove | no | yes |

**Idempotent** means repeating the request has the same effect as sending it once (DELETE twice: still deleted). Clients, proxies and retry logic rely on that; a non-idempotent POST needs an idempotency key to be retried safely. A retry library that resends a timed-out PUT 3 times does no harm; resending a POST 3 times can create 3 orders.

## Status codes that matter

- **200** OK, **201** Created (send a `Location` header with the new resource URL), **204** No Content (successful DELETE or an update with no body).
- **400** Bad Request (malformed or invalid input), **401** Unauthorized (not authenticated: missing or bad credentials), **403** Forbidden (authenticated but not allowed), **404** Not Found, **409** Conflict (duplicate key, stale version), **422** Unprocessable Content (well-formed but semantically invalid; some APIs use it instead of 400 for validation), **429** Too Many Requests (send `Retry-After`).
- **500** for unexpected server failures (never leak internals, topic 10), **503** when temporarily unavailable.

## URLs: routes, params and query strings

```js
const u = new URL(req.url, 'http://localhost');
u.pathname                     // '/users/42'
u.searchParams.get('page')     // '2'  <- a STRING (or null when absent)
new URLSearchParams('tag=a&tag=b').getAll('tag')  // ['a', 'b']
new URLSearchParams('q=x+y').get('q')             // 'x y': + decodes to a space
```

Route parameters (`/users/:id`) and query values are **strings**: convert and validate them (`?page=abc` must be a 400, not `NaN` reaching the database). Path segments are percent-encoded: `decodeURIComponent('caf%C3%A9')` is `'café'`, and malformed encodings throw a `URIError`, which is also a 400.

## Middleware

Frameworks like Express run middleware **in registration order**: each one handles the request or calls `next()`. Order matters: body parsing before handlers that read the body, authentication before authorisation, the 404 handler after every route, and the **error handler last**. In Express an error handler is recognised by its four parameters `(err, req, res, next)`; any `next(err)` (or, in Express 5, a rejected async handler) jumps straight to it.

## Validate at the boundary

Parse, validate and normalise once, at the edge: types of every field, required fields, string lengths, enum values, number ranges. Respond 400 (or 422) with field-level messages. **Allow-list** fields: never `Object.assign(user, req.body)`, which lets a client set `role: 'admin'` (mass assignment).

## Pagination

- **Offset**: `?limit=20&offset=40`. Simple, but slow for deep pages and unstable while rows are inserted.
- **Cursor**: `?limit=20&after=<opaque cursor>` based on a sort key (id or created_at plus id). Stable and fast for infinite scroll.

Always cap `limit` server-side and return a stable sort order.

## Response conventions

`Content-Type: application/json`, a consistent error body (problem details: `{ title, status, detail, errors }`), ISO-8601 timestamps in UTC, and ids as strings. Return 404 rather than 403 for resources the caller must not even know exist.

A client that gets `{ "error": "Not found" }` from one route and `{ "message": "missing" }` from another needs a special case per route. One error shape, served as `application/problem+json` (RFC 9457), lets it handle every failure with the same code.

quiz.prompt: Which methods are idempotent?
choices: GET, PUT and DELETE
GET, POST and DELETE
PUT, POST and PATCH
POST and PATCH
quiz.explanation: Idempotent means sending the same request twice leaves the server in the same state as sending it once. A read changes nothing, a full replacement writes the same representation again, and a second removal finds the resource already gone. POST usually creates a resource or runs an action each time, so a retried POST can create a duplicate order, and PATCH is idempotent only when its body is: `{ "op": "increment" }` is not.

quiz.prompt: A POST /orders succeeds. Which response is most correct?
choices: 200 OK with the newly created order in the response body
204 No Content with the new order's id in a custom header
201 Created with a Location header for the new order
202 Accepted with a status URL to poll for the new order
quiz.explanation: 201 Created says a new resource exists, and its Location header gives the client the new order's URL; a body with the order is a bonus. 200 is acceptable but less precise, 204 hides the result, and 202 means the work has only been accepted for later processing.

quiz.prompt: A logged-in user requests another tenant's invoice they may not see. What is the usual safest response?
choices: 401, since the user lacks the permission to read that invoice
404, so the response does not reveal it exists
409, since the invoice belongs to another tenant
500, so the error reveals nothing about the invoice
quiz.explanation: 401 means not authenticated. For a resource the caller should not know exists, many APIs answer 404; a 403 is the alternative when its existence is not secret.

quiz.prompt: What does `new URLSearchParams('page=2').get('page')` return?
choices: `null`
`NaN`
quiz.explanation: `URLSearchParams` decodes the query string into text and never guesses types: every value it returns is a string, and `get` returns `null` only when the key is absent. So the number 2 never comes back, and `NaN` appears only once your own code calls `Number()` on a bad value such as `'abc'`. Convert and range-check `page` before it reaches the database.

quiz.prompt: `const p = new URLSearchParams('name=Ada+Lovelace&tag=a%2Bb');` What are `p.get('name')` and `p.get('tag')`?
choices: `'Ada+Lovelace'` and `'a+b'`
`'Ada Lovelace'` and `'a b'`
`'Ada Lovelace'` and `'a+b'`
`'Ada+Lovelace'` and `'a%2Bb'`
quiz.explanation: In a query string (the form-urlencoded format) a bare `+` decodes to a space, while `%2B` is the escaped form of a literal plus, so the values are 'Ada Lovelace' and 'a+b'. A common mistake is to treat both the same way, keeping every plus or turning `%2B` into a space too. Note that `decodeURIComponent` alone leaves `+` as a plus; only the form decoder maps it to a space.

quiz.prompt: In Express, how is an error-handling middleware recognised?
choices: By its function name, which must begin with err
By being registered first, before the routes
By returning a promise that rejects with err
By having four parameters: (err, req, res, next)
quiz.explanation: Express recognises error middleware by its arity: a function with four parameters (err, req, res, next). Register it after the routes so that errors from them reach it. Its name does not matter, and registering it first means it never sees route errors.

quiz.prompt: Why is `Object.assign(user, req.body)` in an update handler dangerous?
choices: It deep-copies req.body, which is slow on big payloads
It lets clients set fields like role or isAdmin
It deletes the user fields that the request body leaves out
It throws whenever req.body contains nested objects or arrays
quiz.explanation: This is mass assignment: every key in the body is copied, including fields such as role or isAdmin that clients must never control. Copy only an explicit allow-list of the fields a client may change.

quiz.prompt: A client sends `?limit=100000`. What should the server do?
choices: Return all 100,000 rows, as the client asked
Cap the limit at a server-side maximum, or reject it
Return a 500, as the value is too large to parse
Ignore pagination and stream the whole table back
quiz.explanation: The server owns the page size: clamp the limit to a maximum (or reject it with 400), because an unbounded limit lets one request read a whole table and overload the database. A large number is perfectly parseable, so a 500 would be wrong.

quiz.prompt: What does `decodeURIComponent("%E0%A4%A")` do?
choices: Returns the input unchanged, because it cannot be decoded
Returns the valid prefix and drops the broken part
Returns null, which a router should turn into a 404
Throws a URIError, which a router should turn into a 400
quiz.explanation: Malformed percent-encoding makes decodeURIComponent throw a URIError, so a router should catch it and answer 400, the client's fault. Left unhandled it becomes a 500. It never returns the input, a prefix or null.

quiz.prompt: Why is cursor pagination preferred for infinite scroll over offset pagination?
choices: It is stable when rows are inserted and fast for deep pages
It needs no sort order, so any query can use it as is
It returns more rows per request than offset pages do
Browsers require cursors for fetch-based infinite scrolling
quiz.explanation: Offset pagination asks the database to skip N rows on every request. When a row is inserted at the top between two requests, everything shifts down by one, so the next page repeats an item; a deleted row makes one get skipped. Skipping also costs time: `OFFSET 100000` reads and discards 100,000 rows. A cursor means start after this sort key, which stays put. It still needs a stable sort order and returns no more rows per page.

flashcards.front: Define idempotent for HTTP.
flashcards.back: Sending the same request many times has the same effect on the server as sending it once.

flashcards.front: 401 versus 403
flashcards.back: 401: the caller is not authenticated (missing or invalid credentials). 403: authenticated, but not permitted to do this.

flashcards.front: When do you return 409?
flashcards.back: When a request conflicts with current state: a duplicate unique value, or an update based on a stale version.

flashcards.front: What type are route params and query values?
flashcards.back: Strings, or null when a query key is absent. Convert and validate them before they reach business logic.

flashcards.front: Why does middleware order matter?
flashcards.back: Each middleware sees only what earlier ones prepared, so parsing comes before handlers, auth before routes, and the error handler last.

flashcards.front: What is mass assignment and how do you prevent it?
flashcards.back: Copying a whole request body onto a model so clients can set privileged fields. Copy only an explicit list of allowed fields.

flashcards.front: Offset versus cursor pagination
flashcards.back: Offset is simple but slow deep down and shifts when rows are inserted; a cursor over a stable sort key is fast and consistent.

flashcards.front: What should a 201 response include?
flashcards.back: A Location header pointing at the new resource, usually with the created representation in the body.

topics.title: React: components, state & hooks
topics.summary: Components as functions of props and state, why state must be replaced rather than mutated, batching and functional updates, keys in lists, lifting state up, derived values, and the rules of hooks.
topics.lesson:
## Components are functions

A React component is a function that takes **props** and returns a description of the UI. React calls it whenever it needs to re-render: when the component's state changes, or its parent re-renders it. Rendering must be **pure**: same props and state, same output, no side effects in the body.

```jsx
function Counter({ step = 1 }) {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  return <button onClick={() => setCount((c) => c + step)}>{count}</button>;
}
```

Props are read-only inputs. A child never changes its props; it asks the parent to, through a callback prop.

## State: replace, never mutate

`useState` gives the current value and a setter. React decides whether to re-render by comparing the new value with the old one using `Object.is`:

```jsx
items.push(newItem); setItems(items);         // same array reference: React may skip the render
setItems([...items, newItem]);                // new array: re-render
setUser({ ...user, name: 'Ana' });            // new object with one field changed
```

Setting a state to an `Object.is`-equal value bails out of the update. Mutating state in place produces stale UI and bugs that are hard to trace.

## Updates are batched; use functional updates

Inside an event handler, React 18 batches every setter call and re-renders once afterwards. A setter does not change the variable in the current render:

```jsx
setCount(count + 1);
setCount(count + 1);    // both read the same count: +1 in total
setCount((c) => c + 1);
setCount((c) => c + 1); // updater functions chain: +2
```

Use the updater form whenever the next state depends on the previous one. Since React 18 the batching also applies in timeouts, promises and native event listeners: three setter calls inside a `setTimeout` still cause one render.

## Lists need stable keys

`{orders.map((o) => <OrderRow key={o.id} order={o} />)}`. Keys tell React which item is which between renders. Using the array **index** as key breaks when items are inserted, removed or reordered: state (an input's text, a checkbox) sticks to the wrong row. Keys must be stable and unique among siblings.

## Lifting state up and derived values

When two components need the same data, move the state to their closest common parent and pass it down with callbacks. Do not copy props into state, and do not store what you can compute: a filtered list, a total, `isValid`. Compute it during render (wrap it in `useMemo` only if it is measurably expensive).

## Controlled inputs

`<input value={name} onChange={(e) => setName(e.target.value)} />`: the state is the single source of truth, and every keystroke flows through it, which makes validation and formatting straightforward.

The alternative is an uncontrolled input with `defaultValue` and a ref, where the DOM holds the text and you read it on submit. Starting with `useState()` and later setting a string flips the input from uncontrolled to controlled, and React warns about it; start with `useState('')`.

## The rules of hooks

1. Call hooks only at the **top level** of a component or custom hook: never inside conditions, loops or after an early return. React identifies each hook by its call order.
2. Call hooks only from React functions (components and custom hooks named `useSomething`).

## useReducer for complex state

When updates involve several fields or many kinds of events (a cart, a multi-step form), `useReducer(reducer, initial)` centralises the logic in a **pure** function `(state, action) => newState`, which is easy to test without rendering anything: `assert.deepEqual(cartReducer(state, { type: 'clear' }), { items: [] })` is a complete test.

## React 19: what changed

- **Actions.** An async function passed to `startTransition` or to a form's `action` prop is an Action: React tracks its pending state, errors and optimistic updates. `const [state, formAction, isPending] = useActionState(saveAction, initialState)` wires one to a form; `useFormStatus` reads the pending state from inside the form, and `useOptimistic` shows the expected result until the server answers.
- **`use`.** `use(promise)` reads a promise (the component suspends until it settles) and `use(Context)` reads context. Unlike other hooks, `use` may be called inside conditions and loops.
- **`ref` is a prop.** Function components receive `ref` like any other prop, so `forwardRef` is no longer needed in new code. A ref callback may return a cleanup function.
- **`<Context>` is the provider.** Render `<ThemeContext value="dark">` instead of `<ThemeContext.Provider>`.

The rules on this page (immutable state, keys, the rules of hooks) are unchanged.

quiz.prompt: Inside one click handler: `setCount(count + 1); setCount(count + 1);` with count 0. What is count after the re-render?
choices: It throws
quiz.explanation: `count` is a constant inside this render: the setter does not change it, it queues an update for the next render. Both calls compute `0 + 1` and queue "set to 1", so the result is not 2. React batches the two calls and renders once, and setting state twice is not an error. The updater form, `setCount((c) => c + 1)`, receives the queued value each time and chains to 2.

quiz.prompt: Why might `items.push(x); setItems(items);` fail to update the UI?
choices: push throws on arrays that React holds in component state
setItems needs an updater function whenever it is given an array
The reference is unchanged, so React can skip the update
React compares state arrays by their length, not by reference
quiz.explanation: React decides whether state changed with `Object.is(old, next)`, which for objects compares references. `push` changes the array in place, so `setItems(items)` passes the very same array and React may treat it as unchanged and do nothing. push does not throw, arrays need no updater function, and React never compares lengths. Create a new array, `setItems([...items, x])`, so the reference changes.

quiz.prompt: Why is the array index a poor `key` for a list where rows can be removed?
choices: Index keys make React re-create every row on each render
Indexes shift on removal, so React reuses the wrong row's state
Index keys trigger a dev warning that also fails production builds
React ignores numeric keys and warns about duplicates
quiz.explanation: React matches list children between renders by key. With index keys, removing the first row gives the old second row key 0, so React keeps the state and DOM of slot 0 and hands them to the next item: a typed draft or a checked box shows up on the wrong row. Index keys do not force every row to be re-created, and they trigger no warning or build failure. Use a stable id from the data.

quiz.prompt: Which follows the rules of hooks?
choices: Calling useState inside an if block that checks a prop
Calling useEffect once per item inside a for loop
Calling useState after an early return for loading states
Calling every hook unconditionally, at the top level
quiz.explanation: React stores a component's hooks as a list and matches each call to its slot purely by call order. A hook inside an `if`, inside a loop, or after an early return runs on some renders and not on others, so later hooks read another hook's state, and React warns or throws ("Rendered more hooks than during the previous render"). Put the condition inside the hook, such as inside the effect body, and return early only after every hook has run.

quiz.prompt: Two sibling components both need the selected customer. Where should that state live?
choices: In both siblings, kept in sync with effects
In their closest common parent, passed down as props
In a module-level variable that both siblings import
In the first sibling, which passes it to the other
quiz.explanation: Lift the state to the closest common parent and pass it down as props, so there is one source of truth. Two copies kept in sync with effects drift and render twice, a module variable does not trigger re-renders, and siblings cannot pass props to each other.

quiz.prompt: A component shows `orders.filter((o) => o.status === tab)`. Should the filtered list be stored in state?
choices: No: derive it during render from the existing state
Yes: state is the right place for any list shown
Yes, kept in sync by a useEffect on orders and tab
Yes, once the list grows past ten items
quiz.explanation: Anything computable from state and props on every render is not state of its own. Copying the filtered list into state creates a second copy that must be kept in sync, and a `useEffect` that does the syncing renders once with stale data and then again with the fixed list. The size of the list does not change the rule. Reach for `useMemo` only when profiling shows the filter is expensive.

quiz.prompt: What does React do when you call a state setter with a value `Object.is`-equal to the current state?
choices: Re-renders the whole tree from the root
Logs a redundant-update warning in the console
Bails out: no re-render is needed
Resets the component's state to its initial value
quiz.explanation: The setter compares the new value with the current one using `Object.is`. Equal means nothing changed, so React skips the update for that component and its children. It does not re-render from the root, log a warning or reset state to its initial value. React may still call the component function once before it bails out, but it discards that result and leaves the children alone.

quiz.prompt: What must a component body NOT do while rendering?
choices: Read props passed in by its parent
Call hooks such as useState, useMemo or useRef
Return JSX built from props and state
Perform side effects such as fetching data
quiz.explanation: React may call a component many times and throw a render away; Strict Mode even calls it twice in development to expose impure code. So the body must compute JSX from props and state and nothing else. A fetch in the body fires on every render, and a setState after it can loop forever. Reading props, calling hooks at the top level and returning JSX are all normal; side effects go in event handlers or `useEffect`.

quiz.prompt: What makes an input "controlled"?
choices: Its value comes from state and onChange updates it
It has a ref that React uses to read its current value
It is disabled, so the user cannot change its value
It sets defaultValue from state on the first render
quiz.explanation: A controlled input renders whatever its `value` prop says. Each keystroke fires `onChange`, the handler sets state, and React renders the input with the new value; if the handler does not set state, React puts the old text back. An input read through a ref, or one seeded with `defaultValue`, is uncontrolled: the DOM owns its value. Disabling an input is a separate matter.

quiz.prompt: Why is a reducer for useReducer written as a pure function?
choices: Because React runs reducers in a separate Web Worker thread
Because reducers are serialised and sent to the server
So the next state depends only on the state and the action
So React can skip calling it when the action repeats
quiz.explanation: Pure reducers can be tested in isolation and replayed; mutation inside them causes the same stale-UI bugs as mutating state. That makes it predictable and easy to test.

flashcards.front: How does React decide a state update changed something?
flashcards.back: It compares the new value with the old one using Object.is, so a mutated object or array looks unchanged.

flashcards.front: Why use the updater form of a state setter?
flashcards.back: Updater functions receive the latest pending state, so several updates in one handler chain correctly instead of overwriting each other.

flashcards.front: What are list keys for?
flashcards.back: They let React match items between renders. Keys must be stable and unique among siblings, typically a database id.

flashcards.front: What does lifting state up mean?
flashcards.back: Moving shared state to the nearest common parent and passing it, plus callbacks to change it, down as props.

flashcards.front: Why not store derived values in state?
flashcards.back: They can drift from their source. Recompute them during render, memoising only when the computation is expensive.

flashcards.front: The two rules of hooks
flashcards.back: Call hooks unconditionally at the top level, and only from components or custom hooks.

flashcards.front: When reach for useReducer over useState?
flashcards.back: When state has several related fields or many kinds of updates, so one pure reducer function owns all transitions.

flashcards.front: What does purity mean for a component?
flashcards.back: For the same props and state it returns the same output and has no side effects while rendering.

topics.title: React: effects, rendering & data fetching
topics.summary: When effects run, dependency arrays compared with Object.is, cleanup order, StrictMode double runs, stale closures, race conditions in fetch effects, and the effects you should not write at all.
topics.lesson:
## When effects run

`useEffect(fn, deps)` runs `fn` **after** React has committed the render to the screen, never during rendering. Then:

- no dependency array: after EVERY render
- `[]`: after the first render only (and its cleanup on unmount)
- `[a, b]`: after the first render, and after any render where `a` or `b` changed, compared with `Object.is`

If `fn` returns a function, that is the **cleanup**. React runs the previous cleanup **before** running the effect again, and on unmount. Subscriptions, timers, sockets and fetches all need cleanup.

```jsx
useEffect(() => {
  const id = setInterval(tick, 1000);
  return () => clearInterval(id);
}, []);
```

In development, **StrictMode** mounts, unmounts and re-mounts every component once, so each effect runs, cleans up, and runs again. An effect that breaks when run twice was already broken (it would leak or double-subscribe on fast navigation).

## Dependencies: Object.is all the way down

Objects, arrays and functions created during render are NEW every render, so an effect depending on them re-runs every time, and an effect that sets state from them can loop forever:

```jsx
const options = { userId };                  // new object each render
useEffect(() => { load(options); }, [options]);   // runs after every render
useEffect(() => { load({ userId }); }, [userId]);  // depend on the primitive instead
```

`useMemo` and `useCallback` keep a value or function identity stable between renders when it must be a dependency. `NaN` as a dependency is stable (`Object.is(NaN, NaN)` is true); `0` and `-0` count as different.

## Stale closures

An effect or callback sees the props and state of the render that created it. An interval created once with `[]` that reads `count` keeps reading the FIRST render's `count` forever. Fixes: include the value in the dependencies, use the updater form `setCount((c) => c + 1)`, or keep a mutable `useRef`.

## Fetching in an effect: the race condition

```jsx
useEffect(() => {
  const ac = new AbortController();
  fetch(`/api/users/${id}`, { signal: ac.signal })
    .then((r) => r.json())
    .then(setUser)
    .catch((e) => { if (e.name !== 'AbortError') setError(e); });
  return () => ac.abort();   // id changed or unmounted: ignore the stale response
}, [id]);
```

Without cleanup, a slow response for an OLD id can arrive after the new one and overwrite it. When a request cannot be aborted, use a flag instead: `let ignore = false;` in the effect, `if (!ignore) setUser(u)` in the callback, and `ignore = true` in the cleanup. In real apps a data-fetching library (TanStack Query, SWR) or the framework's loaders handle caching, deduping and races for you.

## You might not need an effect

- **Derived values**: compute during render (topic 19), not `useEffect(() => setFull(first + last), [first, last])`.
- **Responding to an event**: put the logic in the event handler, not in an effect watching a "submitted" flag.
- **Resetting state when an id changes**: give the component `key={id}` so React remounts it with fresh state.

Effects are for synchronising with things OUTSIDE React: the network, timers, the DOM, browser APIs, third-party widgets.

## Rendering, briefly

A state change re-renders that component and, by default, all of its children. Re-rendering is usually cheap; only optimise (`React.memo`, `useMemo`, moving state down, splitting components) when the profiler shows a real cost. Never mutate during render, and keep keys stable so React can preserve the right state.

## React 19 and the React Compiler

The React Compiler (a build plugin, stable since late 2025) memoizes components and computed values automatically. In a compiled codebase most hand-written `useMemo`, `useCallback` and `React.memo` calls become unnecessary, but effects do not change: dependencies, cleanup and the fetch race above still apply. The compiler relies on the rules of React (pure render, no mutation of props or state), and code that breaks them is skipped or misbehaves. For data loading, React 19 adds `use(promise)` with Suspense as an alternative to fetching in an effect, usually through a framework or a data library that caches the promise.

quiz.prompt: When does an effect with dependency array `[]` run?
choices: Before the first render, and again before unmount
After the first render only, with its cleanup on unmount
After every render, with its cleanup before the next one
Only after a state change triggers a re-render
quiz.explanation: React runs effects after it has committed a render to the screen, never before it. With `[]` there is nothing to compare, so after the first commit no dependency can ever count as changed and the effect is not run again; its cleanup runs once, when the component unmounts. A state change re-renders the component without re-running this effect. Omitting the array is what makes an effect repeat.

quiz.prompt: When does an effect with NO dependency array run?
choices: After every render
Only on mount
Only on unmount
Only when state changes
quiz.explanation: With no array, React has no previous values to compare, so it treats each commit as a reason to run the effect again. That includes renders caused by a parent, not only by this component's state changes, so a state-only rule is too narrow. Running just on mount is what `[]` does, and no effect runs only on unmount: that is the job of the function it returns.

quiz.prompt: In what order do the cleanup and the next run of an effect happen when its dependencies change?
choices: The new effect runs, then the old cleanup
They run in parallel on separate threads
The old cleanup runs first, then the new effect
The cleanup waits until the component unmounts
quiz.explanation: When a dependency changes, React first calls the function returned by the previous run, which still sees the old values its closure captured, and only then runs the effect with the new values. So an old subscription is closed before its replacement opens, and the two never overlap. It all happens on the one JavaScript thread, nothing runs in parallel, and nothing waits for unmount; unmount is just the final cleanup.

quiz.prompt: `const opts = { id }; useEffect(() => load(opts), [opts]);` What happens?
choices: It runs only when id changes, because opts wraps it
It runs once, because opts is created on the first render
React warns that opts is an object and skips the effect
It runs after every render, because opts is new each time
quiz.explanation: `{ id }` creates a new object during each render, and React compares every dependency with `Object.is`, which for objects compares identity. The new `opts` is never identical to the last one, so the effect counts as changed on each commit even when `id` stayed the same. React does not look inside objects, does not warn and does not skip the effect. Depend on `id` itself, or build `opts` with `useMemo`.

quiz.prompt: Why does an effect run twice on mount in development?
choices: A known bug in React 18 that development builds still have
StrictMode remounts each component to expose missing cleanup
Hot reloading mounts each component twice on startup
Omitted dependencies make React run the effect twice
quiz.explanation: In development, `<StrictMode>` simulates an unmount and a second mount right after the first one: React runs each effect, runs its cleanup, and runs it again. An effect with a correct cleanup ends in the same state either way, while a missing cleanup shows up as a doubled subscription or request. It is deliberate, not a bug, and unrelated to hot reloading or omitted dependencies. Production builds skip the extra cycle.

quiz.prompt: A user switches from user 1 to user 2 quickly, and user 1's slow response arrives last. Without cleanup, what is shown?
choices: User 1's data, overwriting user 2
User 2's data, the one requested last
A React race-condition warning
Nothing until the user switches again
quiz.explanation: Both requests are in flight, and each `.then(setUser)` runs whenever its own response arrives. User 2's answer comes first and is shown; then user 1's slow answer arrives and its `setUser` overwrites it, so the screen shows user 1 while the URL says user 2. React does not detect the race and shows no warning. The cleanup fixes it: abort the old request, or set an `ignore` flag that the stale callback checks.

quiz.prompt: An interval set up with `[]` deps logs `count` every second while count changes. What does it log?
choices: The latest count, read fresh from state at each tick
undefined, once the first render is gone
The count from the first render, every time
A count that lags one render behind
quiz.explanation: The interval callback is created once, by the effect of the first render, and it closes over that render's `count`. Later renders create new `count` constants, but the interval never sees them, so it keeps logging the first value: a stale closure. The value does not turn into undefined and does not lag one render behind; it stays frozen. Fix it with `count` in the dependencies, a ref, or the updater form.

quiz.prompt: Which is NOT a good use of useEffect?
choices: Subscribing to a WebSocket and closing it on cleanup
Starting a timer that the cleanup clears
Syncing with a third-party chart library
Computing fullName from firstName and lastName
quiz.explanation: Effects are for synchronising with systems outside React: a WebSocket, a timer or a third-party chart library all need setup and cleanup. `fullName` is just `firstName + ' ' + lastName`, computable while rendering. Putting it in state set by an effect renders once with the old name, runs the effect, and renders again: an extra render and a frame of inconsistent UI. Compute derived values in the component body.

quiz.prompt: How do you reset a form component's state when the edited record id changes?
choices: Render it with key={id} so React remounts it
Change the id prop; React resets state on its own
Store the id in a ref so the form re-renders
Wrap the initial state in useMemo with [id]
quiz.explanation: React keeps a component's state as long as the same component type stays at the same position with the same key. Changing a prop leaves that state alone, so the form would keep the old record's edits. A new key tells React this is a different component: it unmounts the old one and mounts a new one with fresh initial state. A ref change triggers no render, and `useMemo` only caches a value; neither resets `useState`.

quiz.prompt: Is a dependency of `NaN` treated as changed on every render?
choices: Yes: NaN !== NaN, so it changes
No: Object.is(NaN, NaN) is true
In StrictMode yes, in production no
React rejects NaN as a dependency
quiz.explanation: React compares each dependency with `Object.is`, not with `===`. The two differ in exactly two cases: for NaN, `===` says unequal while `Object.is` says equal, and for `0` versus `-0`, `===` says equal while `Object.is` says different. So a NaN dependency is stable, the same in StrictMode and in production, and React accepts it like any other value.

flashcards.front: The three dependency-array cases of useEffect
flashcards.back: No array: it re-runs following each render. Empty array: once after mount. With values: after mount and whenever a value changed by Object.is.

flashcards.front: When does an effect cleanup run?
flashcards.back: Before the effect runs again with new dependencies, and when the component unmounts.

flashcards.front: Why do objects and functions make troublesome dependencies?
flashcards.back: They are recreated on every render, so they always look changed. Depend on primitives or keep their identity with useMemo or useCallback.

flashcards.front: What is a stale closure in React?
flashcards.back: A callback or effect that keeps reading the props and state of the render that created it, because it was never recreated.

flashcards.front: How do you avoid race conditions when fetching in an effect?
flashcards.back: Abort the request or set an ignore flag in the cleanup, so a response for outdated inputs is never applied.

flashcards.front: Why does StrictMode run effects twice in development?
flashcards.back: To surface effects without proper cleanup; a correct effect behaves the same after a mount, unmount and remount.

flashcards.front: Three effects you usually do not need
flashcards.back: Computing derived data, reacting to user events (use the handler), and resetting state on a prop change (use a key).

flashcards.front: What are effects actually for?
flashcards.back: Synchronising a component with systems outside React: network, timers, subscriptions, the DOM and browser APIs.

topics.title: SQL queries: NULLs and joins
topics.summary: Three-valued logic and the rows it silently drops, deterministic ORDER BY and LIMIT, inner versus left joins, GROUP BY and HAVING, and the fan-out that double-counts totals.
topics.lesson:
## NULL means unknown

SQL logic has three values: true, false and unknown. Any comparison with NULL (`= NULL`, `<> 'void'`, `< 5`) is unknown, and `WHERE` keeps only rows that are true. So `WHERE status <> 'void'` silently drops every row whose status is NULL. Test with `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL`, or spell it out: `(status IS NULL OR status <> 'void')`. Postgres and SQLite 3.39+ also have `IS DISTINCT FROM`; SQLite also spells it `IS NOT`.

**Failure story.** A support queue listed tickets `WHERE assigned_to <> 42`, meaning "not mine". Every unassigned ticket (NULL) vanished from the screen, and nobody picked them up for a week.

`x NOT IN (1, NULL)` can never be true, so `NOT IN (subquery)` returns nothing as soon as the subquery yields one NULL. Prefer `NOT EXISTS`.

## ORDER BY and LIMIT

Without `ORDER BY`, row order is undefined. With a sort key that is not unique, the order of the ties is undefined too, so `ORDER BY due_date LIMIT 20` can show a row on two pages or on none. End the sort with a unique column: `ORDER BY due_date, id`. Ascending order puts NULLs first in SQLite and last in Postgres; write `NULLS FIRST` or `NULLS LAST` when it matters.

## Joins

- `INNER JOIN` keeps only the pairs that match.
- `LEFT JOIN` keeps every left row; where nothing matches, the right-hand columns are NULL.

A condition on the right table placed in `WHERE` (`WHERE o.status = 'paid'`) rejects those NULL-padded rows, and the left join behaves like an inner join again. Put that condition in `ON`.

## GROUP BY and HAVING

`WHERE` filters rows before grouping; `HAVING` filters groups afterwards. `COUNT(*)` counts rows; `COUNT(col)` counts non-NULL values. After a left join a customer with no orders still has one row, so `COUNT(*)` says 1 where `COUNT(o.id)` says 0. `SUM` over no rows is NULL, not 0: wrap it in `COALESCE(..., 0)`.

```sql
SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS paid_orders
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid'
GROUP BY c.id
HAVING COUNT(o.id) < 3;
```

Group by the key, not the name: two customers called Sam are two groups.

## Fan-out

Joining one parent to two child tables multiplies rows. An order with 3 items and 2 payments becomes 6 rows, so `SUM(p.amount)` is tripled and `COUNT(i.id)` is doubled.

**Failure story.** A revenue report joined orders to payments. A sprint later someone joined line items as well, to add one column. Reported revenue more than doubled overnight, and the figure went into the monthly numbers before anyone checked it against the bank.

`SUM(DISTINCT ...)` is not a repair: two real payments of the same amount collapse into one. Aggregate each child table on its own (a subquery or CTE grouped by the parent key) and join those one-row-per-parent results.

quiz.prompt: A table has 10 rows: 5 with status 'open', 2 with 'void' and 3 where status is NULL. How many rows does `WHERE status <> 'void'` return?
quiz.explanation: For the three NULL rows the comparison `status <> 'void'` is unknown, not true, and WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is true. That leaves the five 'open' rows. Answering 8 treats NULL as a value that differs from 'void'. When the NULL rows belong in the result, say so: `WHERE status <> 'void' OR status IS NULL`.

quiz.prompt: A query with `WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT manager_id FROM staff)` returns no rows, although several ids are plainly not managers. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The subquery returns duplicate manager_id values
NOT IN compares against the first subquery row
NOT IN needs an index on manager_id to match
The subquery returns at least one NULL manager_id
quiz.explanation: With a NULL in the list, `id NOT IN (...)` is unknown for every id that is not in it, so no row passes. NOT EXISTS does not have this trap.

quiz.prompt: A list is paged with `ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 20 OFFSET 20`, and many rows share one created_at. What can go wrong?
choices: The database rejects LIMIT when the sort key has duplicates
Tied rows can appear on two pages, or on neither page
Rows with the same created_at are merged into one row
OFFSET is applied before the sort, so page two is unsorted
quiz.explanation: When many rows share one created_at, the sort leaves their order undefined, and two executions of the query may break the tie differently. A row can then show on page one and again on page two while another is skipped. Nothing is merged or rejected: the database may return ties in any order. Add a unique tiebreaker, `ORDER BY created_at, id`.

quiz.prompt: A query reads `FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.status = 'paid'`. Which customers does it return?
choices: Every customer, with NULL order columns where none is paid
Customers that have at least one paid order
Customers that have no paid order at all
Every customer exactly once, whatever their orders
quiz.explanation: For a customer without orders o.status is NULL, the WHERE test is unknown and the row is dropped. Moving the status test into ON keeps every customer.

quiz.prompt: After `customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ... GROUP BY c.id`, what do `COUNT(*)` and `COUNT(o.id)` report for a customer with no orders?
choices: `NULL` and `0`
quiz.explanation: The outer join keeps the customer and fills the order columns with NULL, so that customer still owns one joined row and COUNT(*) gives 1. COUNT(o.id) counts only non-NULL values, and the single o.id is NULL, so it gives 0. Neither aggregate answers NULL here. After an outer join, count related rows with COUNT(o.id).

quiz.prompt: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
choices: WHERE filters joined tables; HAVING filters the first table in FROM
WHERE runs after GROUP BY; HAVING runs before it, on the raw rows
WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters the groups
WHERE accepts any expression; HAVING accepts column names
quiz.explanation: WHERE is applied to each row before GROUP BY forms the groups, and HAVING is applied to the groups afterwards. That is why HAVING can test an aggregate such as `COUNT(o.id) < 3`, which does not exist yet while WHERE runs. The order is not the other way round, and neither clause is limited to one table or to bare column names.

quiz.prompt: An order has 3 line items and 2 payments of 50 each. A query joins orders to both tables, groups by order and selects `SUM(p.amount)`. What does it return for this order?
quiz.explanation: Each join multiplies the rows: the order's 3 line items times its 2 payments give 6 joined rows, and every one of them carries a payment of 50. SUM adds 50 six times, so the answer is 300 rather than the real 100. Every payment is counted once per line item, which is why each child table is aggregated before it is joined.

quiz.prompt: Why is `SUM(DISTINCT p.amount)` a poor repair for a total inflated by a second join?
choices: DISTINCT is ignored inside aggregates, so the total stays inflated
It forces a full table scan, because DISTINCT cannot use an index
It sums each distinct order id in place of the payment amounts
Two genuine payments of the same amount would be counted once
quiz.explanation: DISTINCT inside SUM removes equal values, not duplicated rows. If an order really has two payments of 50, `SUM(DISTINCT p.amount)` gives 50 and silently loses one of them. DISTINCT is not ignored inside aggregates, so the total does not stay inflated: it becomes wrong in the other direction. Aggregate the payments per order in a subquery and join that result instead.

quiz.prompt: `orders` has 4 rows whose `discount` is 10, 20, NULL and NULL. What does `SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(discount), AVG(discount) FROM orders` return?
quiz.explanation: COUNT(*) counts rows (4), COUNT(discount) skips NULLs (2), and AVG also ignores NULLs, so it is (10 + 20) / 2 = 15. The tempting 7.5 treats NULL as 0; write COALESCE(discount, 0) if that is what the report really means.

quiz.prompt: Which rows does `SELECT p.name, r.id FROM products p LEFT JOIN reviews r ON r.product_id = p.id AND r.stars = 5` return?
choices: Only products that have at least one 5-star review
Every product; review columns are NULL where it has no 5-star review
Only the products that have no reviews at all
Every product exactly once, whatever its reviews
quiz.explanation: A condition in the ON clause of a LEFT JOIN only decides which reviews match; every product row is kept, with NULLs when nothing matched. Moving `r.stars = 5` into WHERE would drop those rows. A product with two 5-star reviews appears twice, so "exactly once" is wrong.

flashcards.front: Why does `WHERE col <> 'x'` skip rows where col is NULL?
flashcards.back: A comparison with NULL is unknown, and WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is true. Add `OR col IS NULL` when those rows belong in the result.

flashcards.front: How do you make `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` deterministic?
flashcards.back: End the sort with a unique column such as the primary key, so ties always come out in the same order.

flashcards.front: LEFT JOIN: where does a condition on the right-hand table go?
flashcards.back: In the ON clause. In WHERE it rejects the NULL-padded rows and the join behaves like an inner join.

flashcards.front: `COUNT(*)` versus `COUNT(col)`
flashcards.back: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) counts rows where col is not NULL. After a left join, count the right table's key to get a real zero.

flashcards.front: What is join fan-out?
flashcards.back: Joining a parent to two child tables repeats each child row once per row of the other child, so sums and counts come out multiplied.

flashcards.front: How do you fix a total that fan-out has inflated?
flashcards.back: Aggregate each child table separately by the parent key, then join those one-row-per-parent results to the parent.

topics.title: SQL schema design and constraints
topics.summary: Primary and foreign keys, NOT NULL, UNIQUE and CHECK as the last line of defence, what normalisation protects, and keeping a unique rule alive next to soft delete.
topics.lesson:
## Keys

Every table needs a primary key: a value that identifies one row and never changes. A generated id (integer or UUID) is the safe choice, because business values that "never change" (an email, a SKU) do. Enforce the business rule separately, with `UNIQUE`.

## Constraints are the last line of defence

A check in application code races. Two requests both ask "is this email taken?", both see no row, both insert. Only the database sees every writer, so the rule belongs there.

- `NOT NULL`: a value is required.
- `UNIQUE`: no two rows are equal. NULLs count as different from each other, so a nullable unique column accepts many NULLs. Pair it with `NOT NULL`.
- `CHECK (qty > 0)`: a rule for one row. A check fails only when it is false; with a NULL input the result is unknown and the row passes.
- `REFERENCES users(id)`: a foreign key. No orphan rows, and by default a parent that still has children cannot be deleted. `ON DELETE CASCADE` deletes the children with it: choose that on purpose, never by habit.

**Failure story.** Sign-up checked the email in code. A double-click sent two requests a few milliseconds apart and both passed the check. Two accounts shared one email, and "reset password" opened whichever row the query happened to return first.

SQLite enforces foreign keys only on a connection where `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON` has run (the SQLite library defaults to off; Node's `node:sqlite` turns it on). Postgres always enforces them.

## Normalisation

Store each fact once. If every order row carries a copy of the customer's email, a change of address updates one place and leaves the others stale. Put the fact in one table and point at it with a foreign key.

A copy is correct when it records history. The price paid belongs on the order line.

**Failure story.** Order lines stored only `product_id`, and invoices computed totals from the current `products.price`. The January price rise silently changed every past invoice, and the totals no longer matched what customers had paid.

## Soft delete and unique rules

Setting `deleted_at` in place of deleting a row keeps history, at a cost: every query must filter `deleted_at IS NULL`, and a plain `UNIQUE (email)` now stops a person from signing up again with the email of a deleted account. `UNIQUE (email, deleted_at)` does not help: live rows have a NULL there, NULLs are distinct, and two live rows with one email pass.

Use a partial unique index, which covers only the rows that match its `WHERE`:

```sql
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_email_live
ON users (email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;
```

SQLite and Postgres both support this; MySQL does not. The same tool enforces "at most one row of this kind per parent", such as one primary address per customer.

quiz.prompt: A column is declared `email TEXT UNIQUE` and allows NULL. By default, how many rows with a NULL email can the table hold in SQLite and in Postgres?
choices: None, because UNIQUE implies NOT NULL
At most one, because NULL equals NULL here
Any number, because NULLs count as distinct
At most one per transaction that inserts them
quiz.explanation: A unique constraint compares values, and a NULL is not equal to another NULL. Add NOT NULL when the value is required. (Postgres 15 can opt in to NULLS NOT DISTINCT.)

quiz.prompt: Sign-up code runs a SELECT to see whether an email is taken and then runs the INSERT. Why is a UNIQUE constraint still needed?
choices: Two concurrent requests can both pass the SELECT before either inserts
A SELECT cannot use an index, so the check is too slow to rely on
A SELECT in a transaction cannot see rows committed before it began
The equality test in a SELECT ignores letter case in every database
quiz.explanation: Check-then-insert is a race between requests: two concurrent sign-ups can both run the SELECT, both see no row, and both insert. Only the database sees both writes, and the UNIQUE constraint refuses the second one at write time. Speed is not the issue, since a lookup on an indexed email is fast, and neither is the visibility of committed rows.

quiz.prompt: A column is `qty INTEGER CHECK (qty > 0)` with no NOT NULL. What happens when a row is inserted with a NULL qty?
choices: It is rejected, because NULL > 0 is not true
It is accepted, because the check is not false
It is accepted, and qty is stored as the number 0
It is rejected, because CHECK implies NOT NULL
quiz.explanation: NULL > 0 is unknown. A CHECK rejects a row only when the expression is false, so the NULL gets in unless the column is also NOT NULL.

quiz.prompt: An enforced foreign key has no ON DELETE clause. What happens when you delete a customer that orders still reference?
choices: The delete is refused with a constraint error
The orders are deleted along with the customer
The orders stay, with customer_id set to NULL
The delete succeeds and the orders are orphaned
quiz.explanation: The default action refuses the delete. Removing the children is ON DELETE CASCADE and clearing the column is ON DELETE SET NULL; both must be asked for.

quiz.prompt: When does SQLite enforce a declared foreign key?
choices: From the moment the table declares REFERENCES
When the table was created with the STRICT keyword
When the write runs inside an explicit transaction
When PRAGMA foreign_keys is ON for the connection
quiz.explanation: SQLite parses REFERENCES but enforces it only while `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON` is set on that connection, and the library leaves it off by default for backward compatibility. A STRICT table or an explicit transaction changes nothing here. Some drivers switch it on for you, node:sqlite among them, so check what your driver does instead of assuming.

quiz.prompt: An order line stores `unit_price`, copied from the product row at purchase time. Is that a normalisation mistake?
choices: Yes: one fact is now stored in two tables and will drift
Yes: a copied column cannot be protected by a foreign key
No: reading the product table is too slow for invoices
No: the price paid is a historical fact of its own
quiz.explanation: The catalogue price and the price paid are different facts. The second must stay fixed when the first changes, so it is stored with the order.

quiz.prompt: A users table has `deleted_at` (NULL while the user is live) and `UNIQUE (email, deleted_at)`. Two live rows are inserted with the same email. What happens?
choices: The second insert fails, because both keys are equal
Both inserts succeed, because the NULLs are distinct
Both succeed, and the first row becomes soft-deleted
The second insert fails once deleted_at is indexed
quiz.explanation: Each key contains a NULL, and a unique constraint treats NULLs as different. A partial unique index over the live rows expresses the real rule.

quiz.prompt: Which declaration enforces "at most one primary address per customer" while allowing any number of non-primary ones?
choices: `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... ON addresses (customer_id, is_primary)`
`CREATE TABLE addresses (..., CHECK (is_primary IN (0, 1)))`
`CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... ON addresses (customer_id) WHERE is_primary = 1`
`CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... ON addresses (is_primary) WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL`
quiz.explanation: The partial index holds only the rows where is_primary = 1, so customer_id must be unique among primary rows and is unrestricted for the rest. A plain UNIQUE (customer_id, is_primary) would also allow just one non-primary address per customer. A CHECK on 0 or 1 limits the values in a row, not how many rows share them.

quiz.prompt: `bookings` declares `CHECK (ends_at > starts_at)`. An app bug inserts a booking whose ends_at equals its starts_at. What happens?
choices: The row is stored: a CHECK only documents the intended rule
The insert fails with a constraint error, whatever the code checked
SQLite swaps the two values so that the check holds
The row is stored with ends_at set to NULL
quiz.explanation: Equal times make `ends_at > starts_at` false, so the database refuses the row with a CHECK constraint error; the constraint holds even when application code forgets the rule. A CHECK is enforced, not documentation, and the database never repairs values for you.

quiz.prompt: Which copied column in an `orders` table is a deliberate snapshot rather than a normalisation bug?
choices: The customer's current display name, refreshed every night
The product's current stock level at the time of each read
The shipping address as it was when the order shipped
The customer's loyalty tier, copied for discount lookups
quiz.explanation: The order must keep the address it actually shipped to, even after the customer moves, so that copy records a historical fact. The other columns copy facts that keep changing; each copy can drift from its source row and give two different answers.

flashcards.front: Why enforce uniqueness in the database and not only in application code?
flashcards.back: Check-then-insert in code races between concurrent requests. The database is the one component that sees every write.
