choices: A read between the two steps puts the old row back until its TTL ends
The delete is refused, since the row is locked until the update commits
The update is rolled back, since the cache and database briefly disagree
The database write is skipped, since the key is already gone from cache
quiz.explanation: Between the delete and the commit, a read that misses loads the old row from the database and stores it again, so the stale value stays until its TTL ends. Nothing is refused or rolled back, and the database write still happens: only the cache is wrong. Write first, then delete the key.

quiz.prompt: With write-then-delete, why can a per-key version check still be needed?
choices: A delete that runs before the commit makes the database lose the update
Cache deletes are queued, so they can run before the write is even sent
Two deletes of one key cancel each other out, so the old cache entry survives
A read that began before the write can store the old row after the delete
quiz.explanation: The slow read loaded the old row, the write committed and deleted the key, then the read stored what it had. Count finished writes per key and skip the store if the count moved.

quiz.prompt: A read-through cache treats entries as fresh while their age is below the TTL. A value stored at t = 1000 ms with a 500 ms TTL is read at t = 1500 ms. What happens?
choices: It is served from the cache, since 1500 ms is still inside the window
It is served stale while a background refresh starts for the next reader
It has expired, so the read loads the value again and stores the result
It has expired, and the read returns undefined until a later load runs
quiz.explanation: At t = 1500 ms the age is exactly 500 ms, which is not below the TTL, so the entry has expired: the read loads the value again and stores the fresh result, rather than serving the old one or returning undefined. A stale-while-revalidate cache would behave differently, but this one has no such rule. An injected clock lets a test hit 1499 and 1500 exactly.

quiz.prompt: A product page is cached under `product:42`, but it is rendered in the caller's currency. What goes wrong?
choices: Nothing: the product id fully identifies the response
Every request misses, because the currencies differ
A euro visitor can get a dollar page cached earlier
The cache keeps a separate entry per currency on its own
quiz.explanation: The key must contain everything that changes the response; the currency is missing, so whichever currency was rendered first is served to everyone until it expires. Caches do not split entries by themselves, so the requests hit, they do not miss.

quiz.prompt: A read-through cache stores an exchange rate with a 60-second TTL. What staleness does it allow?
choices: None: the TTL forces a refresh before each read
A rate up to about 60 seconds behind the source
At most 30 seconds, since entries age on average
Any age, because a TTL is only a hint to evict
quiz.explanation: An entry is served until its age reaches the TTL, so a reader can see a rate almost 60 seconds old; that bound is the promise you choose when picking the TTL. A TTL does not refresh on every read, and averages do not bound the worst case.

flashcards.front: What is cache-aside?
flashcards.back: Read the cache; on a miss load from the database, store the value with a TTL and return it. Writes go to the database and then invalidate the key.

flashcards.front: What belongs in a cache key?
flashcards.back: Every input that changes the response: tenant, user or role when permissions shape it, locale, and the query parameters in a normalised order.

flashcards.front: What is a cache stampede?
flashcards.back: Many requests miss the same hot key at the same moment, often right after it expires, and every one of them runs the expensive load.

flashcards.front: How is single-flight loading built?
flashcards.back: A map from key to the pending promise: a miss checks it first, so concurrent callers await one load. The entry is removed once the promise settles.

flashcards.front: Should a cache keep a failed load?
flashcards.back: No. Waiting callers share the error, then the key becomes loadable again; keeping it would repeat one transient failure for a whole TTL.

flashcards.front: Why invalidate after the database write rather than before?
flashcards.back: Invalidating first leaves a window in which a reader re-caches the old row; after the commit, the next miss reads the new one.

topics.title: N+1 queries and query budgets
topics.summary: Spotting the 1 + N query pattern, fixing it with one batched query per relation, DataLoader-style per-tick loaders, and tests that assert a query budget that does not grow with the data.
topics.lesson:
## What N+1 looks like

```js
const orders = await db.listOrders();                    // 1 query
for (const o of orders) {
  o.customer = await db.customerById(o.customerId);      // + 1 query per order
}
```

One query fetches a list, then the code runs one more query per row. An ORM's lazy relation does the same behind an innocent property access, and a GraphQL resolver per field does it per item. The count grows with the data: 20 orders in a test fixture make 21 queries, and 2,000 in production make 2,001.

## Why it hides until production

With five seed rows and the database on the same machine, 1 + N queries take a few milliseconds. In production every query pays a network round trip, the lists are long, and each request holds a pooled connection for the whole loop.

Failure story: an order history page made 1 + 2N queries (customer and line items per order). It took 12 ms on seed data and 3 seconds for a customer with 400 orders: 801 queries per page view, and a few such users at once drained the connection pool for everyone.

## Batch: one query per relation

Collect the distinct ids, load them with one query (`WHERE id IN (...)`) or a JOIN, put the rows in a `Map` by id, and attach them by lookup. Never zip the results by position: without `ORDER BY` the rows come back in whatever order the database likes, and ids with no row are simply missing. Skip the query for an empty list, because Postgres rejects `IN ()` as a syntax error. Chunk huge lists: databases cap bind parameters per statement, and SQLite's default limit is 32,766.

## Loaders: batching per tick

When the code that needs a row cannot see the whole list (nested resolvers, helpers called per item), use a DataLoader-style loader. Every `load(key)` made in the same tick is collected; then the loader removes duplicates, calls the batch function once with the keys and hands each caller the value at its key's position. The batch function must return exactly one value per key, in key order, with an `Error` for a key that failed.

Failure story: a team made their loader a module-level singleton with a cache. The batching worked, but the cache outlived requests, so a row loaded for one user's request was served to the next user, past their permissions. Create loaders per request.

## Query budgets in tests

Response-time assertions are flaky and do not catch N+1 on small fixtures. Count queries instead: subscribe to the driver's query event (or wrap the client), run the handler for 1, 10 and 200 rows and assert the same small ceiling for each. A count that grows with N is an N+1. A count exactly at the budget passes. When the budget fails, print every query that ran, so the failure message answers "which query repeated?" without a debugger.

quiz.prompt: A handler loads 200 orders with one query, then calls `customerById` once per order. How many queries does one request make?
quiz.explanation: One query fetches the 200 orders, then every order costs one more query: 1 + N = 201. Two is what a batched version makes whatever N is, and 400 would need two lookups per order. The count grows with the data, which is why the problem hides on small fixtures and shows up in production.

quiz.prompt: Why did an N+1 order page look fast in development and slow in production?
choices: Development builds batch the queries automatically while the pool is small
Node caches identical queries in development mode until the next restart
Few seed rows and a local database hide the cost of each query round trip
The ORM turns lazy loading off whenever NODE_ENV is set to development
quiz.explanation: The pattern is the same everywhere; production multiplies it by long lists and a network round trip per query, while holding a pooled connection throughout.

quiz.prompt: In what order does `SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id IN (7, 3, 9)` return its rows when there is no ORDER BY?
choices: In no guaranteed order, and any id without a row is simply absent
In the order of the ids in the IN list, with one row per listed id
In descending id order, because IN sorts its list before it runs
In insertion order, with a NULL row for each id that has no match
quiz.explanation: SQL promises no order without ORDER BY, so the rows may come back in any order: not the order of the IN list, and not sorted descending (SQLite happens to answer 3, 7 here). IN also returns only matching rows, so an id with no customer is simply missing, with no NULL placeholder. Index the result by id in a Map and look each one up.

quiz.prompt: A batching list handler finds that the page has no orders at all. What should it do about the customer query?
choices: Send IN () anyway, since every SQL database treats it as matching nothing
Send IN (NULL), since that list then matches the rows whose id is NULL
Skip it, since an IN list needs at least two values to be valid SQL
Skip it, since Postgres rejects an empty IN list as a syntax error
quiz.explanation: Postgres fails on IN (); SQLite happens to accept it and match nothing. With no ids there is nothing to fetch, so the cheapest correct query is none. IN (NULL) matches no row at all, since comparing with NULL is never true. A one-value list is valid everywhere.

quiz.prompt: A DataLoader-style loader receives `load(1)`, `load(2)` and `load(1)` in the same tick. What does its batch function receive?
quiz.explanation: Keys requested in one tick are de-duplicated and passed once, in the order they were first requested, so the batch function sees one list of two keys. It is tempting to expect every call's key, repeats included, but the second 1 never reaches it, the keys are not wrapped in one array per call, and the order is first-seen, not reversed. Both load(1) calls resolve to the same value.

quiz.prompt: Asked for keys `[5, 8]`, a batch function returns `[row8, row5]`. What does a loader that assigns values by position do?
choices: Gives row8 to load(5) and row5 to load(8), and raises no error at all
Sorts the values by their id first, so each load still gets its own row
Notices the mismatch and rejects both of the loads with a clear error
Gives row5 to both loads, since it is the last row in the result array
quiz.explanation: Position is the whole contract: value i belongs to key i. The batch function, not the loader, must line its results up with the keys.

quiz.prompt: Why should a loader that caches its results be created per request instead of once per process?
choices: A loader keeps a database connection open until it is garbage-collected
Batching needs a live HTTP request, as it hooks into the request socket
Node allows one pending batch per process, so requests would queue behind it
A shared cache serves one user's rows to the next user, past their rights
quiz.explanation: A loader cache that lives for the whole process serves rows loaded for one user to the next user, past their rights, and keeps serving them after the data changes. A per-request loader still batches inside the request, and its cache ends with it. Loaders hold no database connection and need no socket, and Node does not limit a process to one pending batch.

quiz.prompt: Which test assertion reliably catches an N+1 in a list endpoint?
choices: The response for 200 rows arrives in under one second on the CI runner
Each query on its own finishes within 5 ms against the test database
The query count stays at the same ceiling for 1, 10 and 200 rows
Time spent in queries is less than half of the total request time
quiz.explanation: Query counts are deterministic, while timings vary by machine and stay small on small fixtures, so a one-second or 5 ms assertion passes with the N+1 still in place. A count that grows with the row count is the N+1 signature: assert the same ceiling for 1, 10 and 200 rows.

quiz.prompt: A page shows 50 posts, each with its author and its tags. With one batched query per relation, how many queries does it run?
choices: 101: one for posts, one per author, one per tag set
51: the posts, then one per post for both relations
3: posts, authors by id IN (...), tags by post id IN (...)
1, because the ORM always joins every relation
quiz.explanation: Load the page, collect the ids, then fetch each relation once with IN (...): posts, authors and tags make three queries whatever the page size. 101 is the N+1 shape, one query per post per relation, which grows with the page.

quiz.prompt: A test asserts that a list endpoint makes at most 3 queries for 2 rows. Why also run it with 20 rows?
choices: An N+1 grows with the rows, and 1 + 2 still fits that budget
Twenty rows warm the connection pool, so the timing is stable
Budgets count rows rather than queries, so they need more rows
SQLite reports the queries only once there are ten or more rows
quiz.explanation: With 2 rows an N+1 issues 1 + 2 = 3 queries, exactly the budget, so the test passes while the bug is present. With 20 rows it issues 21 and fails. Query counts, not timings, are what make the budget deterministic.

flashcards.front: What is an N+1 query problem?
flashcards.back: One query fetches a list, then the code runs another query per row for related data, so the number of queries grows with the list.

flashcards.front: Fixing an N+1 with a batch query
flashcards.back: Collect the distinct ids, fetch them all in one query, index the rows by id in a Map, then attach each row by lookup.

flashcards.front: Why never match batch-query rows by position?
flashcards.back: Without ORDER BY the database picks the order, and ids that have no row are just missing, so positions do not line up with the request.

flashcards.front: What does a DataLoader-style loader do?
flashcards.back: It gathers every key requested during one tick, drops duplicates, calls the batch function once, and gives each caller the value at its key's position.

flashcards.front: Why does a very large IN list need chunking?
flashcards.back: Databases cap bind parameters per statement (SQLite's default is 32,766), so huge id lists are split across several queries.

flashcards.front: What makes a query-budget test useful?
flashcards.back: It counts queries for several input sizes, asserts one small ceiling for all of them, and on failure prints the queries that ran.

topics.title: Seams, fakes and answerable logs
topics.summary: Injecting the clock and id generator, fakes versus stubs and mocks, characterization tests checked with mutants before a refactor, and structured request logs that answer incident questions without leaking secrets.
topics.lesson:
## Seams: where a test takes control

A seam is a place where behaviour can change without editing the code at that spot (Michael Feathers). A handler's hidden inputs are the clock, id generation and randomness: with `new Date()` or `crypto.randomUUID()` inside it, a test cannot pin the output and can only assert loose ranges. Pass them in instead, `createInvite({ clock, newId, store }, input)`, and read the clock once per operation, so every timestamp of one action comes from the same instant.

Failure story: a billing test computed "one month from now" with the real clock. It passed for months, then failed on the last days of every January: `setUTCMonth` on 31 January 2025 rolls over to 3 March. With an injected clock that date is just another test case.

## Fakes, stubs and mocks

A **stub** returns canned answers. A **fake** is a small working implementation, such as an in-memory repository that keeps rows and enforces uniqueness. A **mock** records calls so the test can assert on them. Prefer fakes for stores and clocks: the test checks outcomes, so a refactor that keeps behaviour keeps the tests green. Mock only where the interaction is the behaviour, such as "exactly one email was sent".

## Characterization tests before a refactor

Before changing untested code, pin what it does today, odd results included: feed inputs and record the outputs as expected values, even where they disagree with the spec. Choose inputs on every decision: the exact threshold, a fractional value where rounding happens, and the combination of flags whose order matters. Then check the suite with mutants: turn `>=` into `>`, `ceil` into `floor`, swap two steps. Each mutant must fail at least one test; typical values such as 20, 80 or whole kilos kill none of them.

Failure story: a shipping-fee clean-up passed its three happy-path tests while turning `subtotal >= 50` into `subtotal > 50`. For a month, orders of exactly 50.00 paid shipping.

## Logs that answer questions

Write one structured JSON line per request: `requestId` (taken from the incoming header or generated at the edge), `tenantId`, `userId`, method, path, status, `durationMs` and a level derived from the status. Then "which tenants saw 500s between 14:02 and 14:10?" is a query, not an afternoon of grep.

Failure story: during an outage the only log line was "error saving order", with no tenant and no request id, and finding the affected customers took a day.

## Never log secrets

Build the line from an allow-list of fields; never spread the request, the headers or the body, because a deny-list misses the next secret someone adds. Strip the query string from logged paths, since reset codes and tokens travel in URLs. Passwords, tokens and the `Authorization` and `Cookie` headers never reach a log.

quiz.prompt: In Michael Feathers' sense, what is a seam?
choices: A place where behaviour can change without editing the code at that spot
A boundary between two modules where all of their shared state is kept
A comment that marks the code which is safe to delete during a refactor
A test that runs the old and the new implementation side by side at once
quiz.explanation: A seam is a place where you can change what the code does without editing it at that spot. Passing a clock or an id generator in as a parameter creates one: a test supplies its own and the handler never changes. It is not a module boundary that keeps shared state, a comment that marks deletable code, or a side-by-side run of two versions.

quiz.prompt: A handler sets `createdAt = new Date().toISOString()`. Why is that a problem for its tests?
choices: toISOString uses local time, so CI and laptops produce different strings
new Date() is cached per process, so every test sees the same instant
A test cannot pin the value, so it can only assert a loose time range
The Date constructor is slower than Date.now, so the tests time out
quiz.explanation: The real clock is a hidden input: the handler reads it, and the test has no way to choose the instant, so it can only assert a loose range. toISOString always formats in UTC, so laptops and CI agree on the format, and new Date() is not cached. Pass a clock in, and the test can assert the exact string.

quiz.prompt: A date is 31 January 2025 (UTC). What does `d.setUTCMonth(d.getUTCMonth() + 1)` turn it into?
quiz.explanation: February 2025 has 28 days, so day 31 of February overflows by three days into March. A real-clock test meets this only on a few days a year; an injected clock makes it a test case.

quiz.prompt: Why prefer an in-memory fake store over a mock that expects an insert call followed by a findById call?
choices: Fakes run inside the database transaction, so their data rolls back by itself
Mocks cannot return promises, so async repositories need a fake instead
A fake records every call, and the test compares them with a golden list
The test then checks outcomes, so a refactor that keeps behaviour stays green
quiz.explanation: A mock pins the call sequence, so changing how the code talks to the store breaks the test even when the result is right. A fake lets the test assert on the state.

quiz.prompt: Before refactoring an untested fee function you write characterization tests. Where do their expected values come from?
choices: From what the code returns today, odd results included
From what the product spec says the fee ought to be
From what the refactored version returns once it is done
From a fresh reimplementation that follows the old docs
quiz.explanation: Characterization tests prove that a refactor changed nothing, so they pin what the code returns today, odd results included. Taking the values from the product spec or from a reimplementation would turn the refactor into a behaviour change, and taking them from the refactored version proves nothing at all. Fixing a wrong result is a separate, deliberate change with its own test.

quiz.prompt: How do you check that a characterization suite is strong enough to refactor behind?
choices: Confirm it reaches full line coverage of the legacy function first
Run it twice and confirm that both runs give the same results
Plant small mutants, like >= turned into >, and see each one fail
Confirm there is at least one test case for each exported function
quiz.explanation: Coverage shows a line ran, not that a change to it would be noticed. A mutant that survives marks a behaviour the suite does not pin.

quiz.prompt: Which kind of logging lets you answer "which tenants saw 500s between 14:02 and 14:10?" with one query?
choices: A free-text line such as "error saving order" written at error level
A stack trace printed to stderr whenever a request handler throws
A count of 500 responses per minute, kept in the process memory
One JSON line per request with tenantId, status, requestId and time
quiz.explanation: Structured fields can be filtered and grouped, so a per-request JSON line answers the question with one query over the time window. A free-text line, a stack trace or an in-memory count of 500s per minute says neither which tenant nor which request was affected, and the counter is gone when the process restarts.

quiz.prompt: Why build a request log line from an allow-list instead of deleting `password` from a copy of the request?
choices: Object spread drops nested fields, so headers never reach the copy anyway
A deny-list misses the next secret field someone adds, like a cookie
Deleting a key from a copy also deletes it from the original request
Log indexes reject lines with unknown keys, so unlisted fields drop anyway
quiz.explanation: With an allow-list a new field stays out until someone decides to log it. Spread is shallow, so nested headers and bodies are copied by reference and would be logged.

quiz.prompt: `function isExpired(token) { return token.exp < Date.now() / 1000; }` is hard to test at the boundary. Which change adds a seam?
choices: Compute Date.now() once, when the module loads
Pass the current time in: isExpired(token, nowSeconds)
Round exp to whole minutes before comparing them
Wrap the comparison in a try/catch that logs errors
quiz.explanation: Taking the time as a parameter lets a test pass the exact second it needs, such as exp itself, with no global patching. Reading the clock once at load still reads the real clock, and rounding or try/catch change behaviour without giving the test control.

quiz.prompt: Which value is safe to put in a request log line?
choices: The request id
The Authorization header
The session cookie value
The password-reset token in the URL
quiz.explanation: A request id identifies the request without granting anything, which is why it belongs on every line. Bearer tokens, session cookies and reset tokens are credentials: anyone who can read the logs could replay them to act as the user.

flashcards.front: What is a seam?
flashcards.back: A point where a test can swap behaviour without editing the code there, such as a clock or id generator passed in as a parameter.

flashcards.front: Why read the clock only once per operation?
flashcards.back: Two readings can differ, so the timestamps of one action disagree; a single reading keeps createdAt and expiresAt consistent and testable.

flashcards.front: Stub, fake and mock
flashcards.back: A stub returns canned answers, a fake is a small working implementation, and a mock records calls so that the test can assert on them.

flashcards.front: What is a characterization test?
flashcards.back: A test that records how untested code behaves now, surprising outputs and all, so that a refactor can prove it changed nothing.

flashcards.front: Which fields make a request log line answerable?
flashcards.back: The ids that locate it (request, tenant, user), what was asked (method and path), the outcome (status and a level derived from it) and how many milliseconds it took.

flashcards.front: What must never reach a log?
flashcards.back: Passwords, tokens, the Authorization and Cookie headers, raw request bodies, and query strings, which can carry reset codes and tokens.

topics.title: Authentication, sessions and tokens
topics.summary: Storing passwords with a slow salted hash, server-side sessions and their cookie flags, what a JWT does and does not protect, and refresh-token rotation with reuse detection.
topics.lesson:
## Storing passwords

Never store a password, and never store a fast hash of one. SHA-256 is built for speed, so a leaked table can be attacked at billions of guesses per second. Use a deliberately slow key-derivation function: scrypt (in `node:crypto`), bcrypt or Argon2, with a random salt per user. The salt makes equal passwords produce different hashes and defeats precomputed tables. Store salt and hash; to verify, recompute and compare with `crypto.timingSafeEqual`. It takes the same time wherever the bytes differ, and it throws when the lengths differ, so compare lengths first.

**Failure story.** A forum stored unsalted MD5. After its database leaked, most passwords were recovered within days, and because people reuse passwords, the attackers went on to those users' email accounts.

## Sessions

After login the server creates a random session id, stores the session itself (user id, expiry) on its side, and sends only the id in a cookie. Logging out deletes the stored session, which takes effect at once. Set the cookie with:

- `HttpOnly`: page scripts cannot read it.
- `Secure`: sent over HTTPS only.
- `SameSite=Lax` or `Strict`: left off cross-site subrequests and form posts (`Strict`: off every cross-site request), which blunts CSRF.

Issue a new session id at login and destroy the old one. Otherwise an attacker who knows the id from before the login shares the session after it. This is session fixation.

**Failure story.** A shop kept the anonymous cart session when a customer signed in. An attacker mailed a link that carried his own session id, the victim signed in on it, and the attacker's browser was now inside her account.

## JWTs

A JWT is three base64url parts: `header.payload.signature`. With HS256 the signature is HMAC-SHA256 over the first two parts, keyed with a server secret. The payload is encoded, not encrypted: anyone holding the token can read it. Verification needs no lookup:

- Fix the algorithm in your code. A token whose header says `"alg":"none"` and carries no signature must be rejected.
- Check the signature before believing any claim.
- `exp` is in seconds. Reject the token once the clock reaches it.

The cost: a JWT cannot be withdrawn before it expires unless the server keeps a list to consult, which is a session store again. So access tokens live for minutes.

## Refresh tokens

A longer-lived refresh token buys new access tokens. Rotate it: each use returns a new refresh token and retires the old one. If a retired token shows up again, it was copied, and you cannot tell the thief from the user. Revoke the whole family, meaning every token that descends from that login, and make the user sign in again. Store only a hash of each refresh token, never the token itself.

quiz.prompt: Why is plain SHA-256 a poor choice for storing passwords, even with a salt?
choices: It is reversible, so a password can be computed back from its hash
It is fast, so an attacker can test guesses at an enormous rate
It is keyed, so every verifying server must share one secret key
It is 256 bits wide, so long passwords collide with the short ones
quiz.explanation: A general-purpose hash is built to be quick, so a salt only stops precomputed tables: guesses against one stolen hash still run at an enormous rate. Cracking hardware tests billions of salted SHA-256 guesses a second, while one default scrypt call takes 16 MB of memory and tens of milliseconds or more. SHA-256 is not reversible and not keyed. Password hashing wants slow: scrypt, bcrypt or Argon2.

quiz.prompt: What does a random salt per user achieve?
choices: Equal passwords get different hashes, so precomputed tables fail
Each guess against one hash takes far longer to compute
The server can decrypt the hash, and an attacker cannot
The password no longer travels to the server at login
quiz.explanation: The salt is stored next to the hash and is not secret. It forces an attacker to attack each user separately; making each guess slow is the job of the slow function.

quiz.prompt: Which cookie attribute stops page JavaScript from reading the session cookie?
choices: `Secure`
`HttpOnly`
`SameSite=Strict`
`Path=/`
quiz.explanation: HttpOnly keeps the cookie out of `document.cookie`, so an injected script cannot read and copy the session id. Secure only makes the browser send the cookie over HTTPS, SameSite=Strict controls whether it goes along on cross-site requests, and Path limits the URLs it is sent to. None of those three hides it from page JavaScript.

quiz.prompt: What is a session fixation attack?
choices: A script injected into the page reads the session cookie and sends it away
The attacker tries every possible value of a short session id until one works
The attacker plants a session id he knows, and the victim then logs in on it
A captured request is replayed after the session behind it has expired
quiz.explanation: The attacker plants an id he knows, for example through a link or a cookie set on a shared machine, and the victim then logs in on it. The id never changes hands after login, because the attacker already has it, which sets it apart from stealing a cookie with an injected script or guessing short ids. Issuing a fresh id at login and destroying the old one ends the attack.

quiz.prompt: Who can read the claims inside an HS256-signed JWT?
choices: Only the server: the payload is encrypted with the signing secret
Nobody: the payload is a one-way hash of the original claims
Only the user: the payload is encrypted with their password hash
Anyone holding the token: the payload is encoded, not encrypted
quiz.explanation: The payload is base64url-encoded JSON, so anyone holding the token can decode the claims without the secret. The HS256 signature protects the claims from being changed, not from being read: nothing is encrypted, and the payload is not a one-way hash. Secrets and personal data do not belong in a JWT.

quiz.prompt: A token arrives with the header `{"alg":"none"}` and an empty signature. What must an HS256 verifier do?
choices: Accept it: an unsigned token is valid while its exp lies in the future
Accept it on read-only routes: integrity matters less for those
Reject it: the verifier fixes the algorithm, the token does not pick it
Reject it when the payload claims an admin role: other roles are harmless
quiz.explanation: The header is attacker-controlled input. An HS256 verifier decides the algorithm itself and rejects anything else, `alg: none` included, on every route and for every role. A verifier that lets the token pick its algorithm lets anyone forge a token by stripping the signature, so an exp in the future or a read-only route changes nothing.

quiz.prompt: A JWT has `exp` 1800000000 and the server clock, in seconds, reads exactly 1800000000. Is the token expired?
choices: Yes: a token is rejected on or after its exp
No: a token is rejected once its exp has passed
No: exp counts milliseconds, so it lasts longer
Yes: exp is the issue time, which has passed
quiz.explanation: RFC 7519 defines exp as the time on or after which the token must not be accepted, in seconds since the epoch, so at exactly 1800000000 it has already expired. A check written as `now > exp` lets it through for one more second. exp is not counted in milliseconds and is not the issue time, which is `iat`.

quiz.prompt: With refresh-token rotation, a refresh token that was already used is presented again. What should the server do?
choices: Issue a new pair of tokens, as the client is retrying a lost response
Reject that one token and leave all of the tokens issued after it valid
Extend the lifetime of the newest token to make up for the failed refresh
Revoke every token descended from that login and require a new one
quiz.explanation: A second use proves the token exists in two places, and the server cannot know which holder is the real user. Issuing a new pair would hand the thief fresh tokens, and rejecting only the reused one leaves the later tokens, possibly the thief's, valid. Revoking the whole family locks both out, and the user simply logs in again.

quiz.prompt: A user changes their password because they suspect someone else is logged in. What should happen to their other server-side sessions?
choices: They stay valid until each one expires on its own
They are deleted, so a stolen session stops working
They are kept but linked to the new password hash
They end only if they are more than a day old
quiz.explanation: Server-side sessions can be revoked at once by deleting them, and a password change after a suspected break-in is exactly when to do it. Leaving them valid lets the intruder keep using a session cookie they already hold, whatever the new password is.

quiz.prompt: Why can a stateless JWT not be revoked before its `exp` without extra server state?
choices: The server checks only the signature and exp, so it has nothing to look up
The signature changes every minute, so old tokens stop working anyway
Revoking it would need the user's password, which the server does not keep
It can: the server sets exp in the past on its copy of the token
quiz.explanation: Verification needs only the secret and the token itself, so a valid token keeps working until exp unless the server adds state such as a deny-list or a per-user token version. The server holds no copy of the token to change, and signatures do not rotate on their own.

flashcards.front: How should passwords be stored?
flashcards.back: As the output of a slow, salted key-derivation function such as scrypt, bcrypt or Argon2, with a random salt per user. Never in plain text or as a fast hash.

flashcards.front: Why compare secrets with a constant-time function?
flashcards.back: An ordinary comparison stops at the first differing byte, and the time it takes leaks how much of a guess was right.

flashcards.front: HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite
flashcards.back: HttpOnly hides the cookie from scripts, Secure restricts it to HTTPS, and SameSite keeps it off cross-site requests (Lax still sends it when a link is followed).

flashcards.front: How do you prevent session fixation?
flashcards.back: Issue a brand-new session id when the user logs in, and invalidate the id that was in use before.

flashcards.front: Session versus JWT: the revocation trade-off
flashcards.back: A server-side session dies the moment its record is deleted. A JWT stays valid until it expires unless the server keeps a list to check, so its lifetime is kept short.

flashcards.front: What is refresh-token reuse detection?
flashcards.back: Each refresh token works once. Seeing a retired one again means it was copied, so the whole token family is revoked.
